summary: The root pictures something bent round until it closes in. In the psalm the pit is a mouth that closes over a man. In Judges the adjective describes men whose right hand is held back, so that they fight with the left. These are skilled warriors who sling with either hand, not men with a disabled hand.

senses.definition: The singer asks to escape the deep before the mouth of the pit closes over him.

This is a man whose right hand is held back from its usual lead, so that he fights with the left. Ehud's left-handed draw lets him carry the sword unseen. The 700 picked Benjamites who are described this way sling at a hair and do not miss. Chronicles describes Benjamites who use both the right hand and the left with stones and arrows.

cognates.gloss: bend, curve; bend into a hoop with the ends brought together; (V) confine oneself, stay in one's house
cognates.note: The bow or twig is bent round until its two ends meet, and figuratively one holds a wrongdoer's hands and bends him to what is right. Form V is used of a woman who keeps to her house or tent. Bending round and closing in fits the pit's mouth closing over the psalmist, and a right hand that is held back.

Hebrew אטר, verb: cognate with Arabic أَطَرَ (to bend, curve)

cognates.gloss: anything that surrounds another thing: hoop, rim, ring
cognates.note: The hoop of a tambourine or sieve, the rim round the lip, and a ring of men camped round a tribe. This is the closed circle that the verb's bending makes, like the mouth of the pit closing round a man.

note: Checked 2026-11-21: SEDRA has no ʾṭr root, and Wiktionary, Oracc and Dillmann give no Aramaic, Akkadian or Ge'ez cognate, so Arabic is the only witness. Later Hebrew keeps both senses: Klein's Mishnaic niphal נֶאְטַר 'was closed', and Jastrow's אִטֵּר 'one whose right hand is tied up or unfit for labour'. The verses in Judges and 1 Ch 12:2 describe skill, so a disabled hand does not fit; the Septuagint's ἀμφοτεροδέξιος ('both-handed') agrees. Possibly there is word-play with בִּנְיָמִין, 'son of the right hand'. Possible link across roots: Arabic إِطَار 'ring round' sits close to עטר 'surround, crown' (36r), which may be an ʾ/ʿ alternation; עצר 'shut up' (39r) is close in meaning. Neither is shown to be the same root.
